chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-baked-or.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, baked or broiled, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are cuts from the dark meat portion of the bird. They are commonly baked or broiled with the skin removed, which reduces fat content. The meat is a rich source of high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron than white meat.
When cooked without skin, a portion of the fat melts away, making the dish lower in calories.
These cuts are staples in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian teriyaki.
Dark chicken meat is juicier because it has higher myoglobin levels.
Proper cooking without skin retains most of the meat’s nutrients.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 25 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health, immunity and bone strength.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Practically carbohydrate‑free, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Reduced saturated fat when skin is removed
items.content: Removing the skin cuts down saturated fat, contributing to a heart‑healthier meal.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F) to ensure safety.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in marinades
items.content: If pre‑marinated in salty solutions, sodium levels can be high.

items.title: Over‑consumption
items.content: Large portions can add excess calories and fat, especially when cooked with added oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake or broil the skin‑less legs, drumsticks and thighs at 180‑200 °C until golden and the juices run clear, basting occasionally. Serve with vegetables, whole grains or slice for salads, soups, stews or sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chicken refrigerated at +2‑+4 °C for up to 2 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Thaw frozen meat in the refrigerator, not at room temperature. Cooked leftovers should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

cornbread-muffin-stick-round-made-from-h.title: Cornbread muffin, stick, round, made from home recipe

content.title: About
content.content: Cornbread muffin is a small baked good made from cornmeal, often enriched with butter, eggs, and milk. In the home recipe (2576) it can be shaped as a stick or a round muffin, featuring a tender crumb and a mildly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornbread has its roots in American cuisine, where it was a staple for Native peoples.
Traditional cornbread muffins are often gluten‑free when made with pure cornmeal.
In the United States, cornbread muffins are commonly served at breakfast with honey or jam.
A small amount of sugar and butter gives the muffin a softer, more aromatic texture.
Shaping the muffin into a stick makes it a convenient on‑the‑go snack.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Cornmeal provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium helps maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other baked goods, cornbread muffins contain a moderate amount of fat, especially when prepared with limited butter.

items.title: Gluten‑free when using pure cornmeal
items.content: Suitable for people with gluten intolerance if no wheat flour is added.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cornbread muffins can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When salt or salty ingredients are added, the sodium level can be high, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cornbread muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and spread with butter, honey, or jam. The stick shape is handy for taking on the go. They pair well with soups, salads, and tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: French toast sticks are ready‑to‑cook strips of bread coated in a mixture of eggs, milk, sugar and spices. When fried they become crispy on the outside and soft inside, making them perfect for breakfast or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic French toast recipe dates back to 19th‑century France as a way to use stale bread.
Sticks are convenient for kids and adults because they are easy to hold and dip.
There are many flavor variations: classic cinnamon, chocolate, berry‑infused, or nut‑topped.
In the United States French toast sticks are often served with maple syrup and fruit sauces.
Pre‑mixed dry blends often include vanilla extract and a pinch of salt to boost flavor.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter provide high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Milk supplies calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish provides B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, the sticks contain no trans fats.

items.title: Mood‑boosting
items.content: Sugar and aromatic spices like cinnamon can promote serotonin production.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: The product contains eggs and milk, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases calories and may be unsuitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Fat when fried
items.content: Cooking in a lot of oil can make the sticks greasy and calorie‑dense.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Made from wheat bread, they are not suitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fry the sticks in a pan or bake them in the oven until golden, then serve with maple syrup, fruit sauce, honey, or a dusting of powdered sugar. They are great for dipping in yogurt or fruit dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry sticks in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked leftovers can be refrigerated for up to 2 days or frozen for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: The frozen yogurt cone with chocolate flavor is a yogurt‑based ice cream coated with a crisp chocolate glaze and served in a waffle cone. It combines the tangy, creamy taste of yogurt with the rich sweetness of chocolate, creating a light and refreshing dessert snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt ice cream contains live probiotic cultures that may support gut microbiota.
The chocolate glaze is often made from dark chocolate, adding antioxidants to the treat.
Waffle cones are typically produced without artificial colors or flavors.
The product is popular in summer, but its lower calorie yogurt base makes it a year‑round choice.
In some countries the cone is served with extra toppings such as nuts, berries, or sprinkles.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: The yogurt component provides live bacterial cultures that can promote digestive health.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Compared with traditional ice cream, yogurt‑based versions usually contain less saturated fat.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Yogurt is a good source of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑Vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Chocolate Antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate glaze is rich in flavonoids, which may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: The product contains dairy; people with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Despite lower calories, the cone still contains added sugar, which can be an issue for diabetics.

items.title: Chocolate Allergy
items.content: The chocolate glaze may contain traces of nuts or soy, which can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Food Additives
items.content: Some versions may include artificial flavorings; check the ingredient list if you avoid them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cone is conveniently eaten by hand straight from the package. You can top it with fresh berries, nuts, or sprinkles for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cone in the freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, the product loses its texture and flavor, so it should be consumed immediately after removal.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft‑serve vanilla frozen yogurt is a dessert made from low‑fat yogurt, cream and natural vanilla extract. It has a creamy texture, a mild tang from the yogurt and a sweet vanilla aroma. The product is served as a soft‑serve swirl and is popular in cafés, food trucks and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt base contains live probiotic cultures that may support gut health.
Real vanilla flavor is often derived from vanilla beans, though many manufacturers use synthetic vanillin.
The soft‑serve texture is achieved by continuous agitation during freezing, preventing large ice crystals.
In some markets, vanilla soft‑serve yogurt is marketed as a healthier alternative to traditional ice cream because of its lower fat content.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: The yogurt component provides live bacteria that can help maintain a balanced intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with regular ice cream, soft‑serve yogurt typically contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy ingredients supply calcium and vitamin D, essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt is a source of riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vanilla antioxidants
items.content: Vanilla contains small amounts of antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains dairy, so individuals with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may be allergic to casein or whey proteins present in yogurt.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sugar is often added for sweetness; those monitoring sugar intake should consider the caloric impact.

items.title: Improper storage
items.content: If stored at too high a temperature, ice crystals can form, degrading texture and flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soft‑serve in cones, cups, or as a scoop in a bowl. Top with fresh berries, nuts, honey, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. It is also used as a base for frozen desserts like milkshakes and smoothie bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, consume within 2–3 days for optimal texture. Thawing may cause the soft‑serve to become grainy.

jam-or-jelly-fruit-juice-sweetened.title: Jam or jelly, fruit juice sweetened

content.title: About
content.content: Jam or jelly is produced by cooking fruit juice with sugar (or another sweetener) and sometimes pectin. The result is a thick, sweet spread that retains the fruit’s aroma and some of its vitamins. It is commonly used as a filling for pastries, toast, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “jam” usually refers to a product that contains fruit pieces, while “jelly” denotes a completely smooth consistency.
Pectin, a natural gelling agent, is found in the skins and seeds of many fruits such as apples and citrus.
In some countries honey is traditionally used instead of sugar to sweeten jam.
Properly sterilized jars allow jam to be stored for several months at room temperature.
There are many regional varieties, e.g., Swedish lingonsylt (lingonberry jam) or Japanese anko (sweet red bean paste).

items.title: Contains vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: The fruit juice in jam retains some vitamin C, B‑vitamins, and polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Source of quick energy
items.content: Sugar (or alternative sweetener) provides a rapid source of glucose, useful for post‑exercise recovery.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Pectin, a soluble fiber, aids regular bowel movements and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Enhances palatability
items.content: The sweet, aromatic flavor makes foods more enjoyable, encouraging a more varied diet.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of added sugar can contribute to weight gain, raise blood glucose levels, and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific fruits used in the jam.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercial products may contain artificial preservatives, colorings, or sweeteners that can be undesirable for sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jam can be spread on bread, rolls, pancakes, used as a filling for cakes, pies, and cheese pancakes, or stirred into yogurt, cottage cheese, or oatmeal for a sweet boost.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store opened jam in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in a tightly sealed jar. It typically keeps for 2‑4 weeks. Prevent contamination and discard if mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Ground veal is finely minced meat from young calves, obtained from tender muscle cuts. It has a light pink color, soft texture, and a delicate flavor characteristic of young beef. It is used in a variety of dishes such as patties, meatballs, sauces, and casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Veal is considered more tender and lower in fat compared to mature beef.
Ground veal is a key ingredient in many traditional European recipes, like Italian ragù and Austrian Wiener schnitzel fillings.
Calves are often fed special diets to enhance the flavor and texture of the meat.
Veal contains less fat than beef but is rich in high‑quality protein and B‑vitamins.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Ground veal provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with regular beef mince, veal has lower saturated fat, making it a better choice for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Veal is a good source of vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Like any raw meat, ground veal can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella; it must be cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef or veal.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Veal contains purines, which can exacerbate gout symptoms in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground veal can be sautéed, braised, baked, or used as a filling for dumplings and pastries. It pairs well with vegetables, herbs, and spices. Avoid overcooking to keep the meat tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground veal in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Ensure the product is fully thawed and odor‑free before cooking.
